name: Polyphasic sleep

lead: Polyphasic sleep means sleeping in several short blocks across 24 hours instead of one night. Online schedules such as Uberman and Everyman aim to cut total sleep to two to four hours, so users have more waking time for training and self-improvement.

Followers time naps to reach REM or deep sleep quickly and rely on adaptation. Segmented nighttime sleep has a documented history in pre-industrial Europe, though a 2015 study of three pre-industrial societies found consolidated nighttime sleep. Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence that extreme reduced-sleep schedules are effective, and a 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus panel report addressed adverse impacts of polyphasic patterns.

paras: People follow a fixed nap timetable, using alarms and strict consistency, and often go through a multi-week adaptation period. Some use milder versions such as biphasic sleep with a night block and an afternoon nap.

Sleep restriction, circadian disruption and microsleeps are the main risks reported by sleep organisations. Sleep loss is also linked to visible effects such as eye bags and puffiness. Driving or operating machinery while sleep-restricted is especially risky.

angle.text: Users try nap-based schedules such as Uberman and Everyman to cut sleep to a few hours and free time for training and other pursuits. Expert panels report adverse impacts, and sleep loss itself shows up in the face as puffiness and eye bags.

lead: Polyphasic sleep is the practice of dividing sleep into several separate periods across 24 hours, usually three or more, rather than one consolidated nighttime block. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement circles, people try schedules such as Uberman and Everyman for a simple reason: fewer hours asleep means more waking hours that can go to the gym, meal prep, skincare routines and other appearance work. Lifting forum posters have also asked whether multiple naps could deliver recovery for training in less time.[1][2]

The term was used in the early twentieth century by psychologist J. S. Szymanski to describe animal activity patterns.[1] Historical research suggests segmented nighttime sleep was common in pre-industrial Europe, a view argued by historian A. Roger Ekirch in 2001, though a 2015 study of three pre-industrial societies found monophasic nighttime sleep and Ekirch has questioned its conclusions.[1]

Research on extreme schedules is limited. A 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus panel reviewed 22 papers and reported no evidence of benefit from polyphasic schedules, associating the sleep deficiency they involve with adverse physical, mental and performance outcomes.[3] A 2024 study of ten young adults on a radical six-nap schedule reported that growth hormone release was abolished, a hormone relevant to the recovery and body-composition goals many practitioners care about.[4]

paras: Everyman uses roughly three hours of core sleep plus three 20-minute naps; Uberman uses a nap about every four hours totalling about three hours; the Buckminster Fuller pattern used 30-minute naps every six hours.[1] Grokipedia also lists Dymaxion and biphasic variants.[2]

Ekirch documented references to a 'first sleep' and 'second sleep' separated by waking.[1] Buckminster Fuller reportedly kept intermittent sleeping for two years in the 1940s, a 1943 Time article said, and stopped because it conflicted with his associates' schedules.[1] Claudio Stampi studied polyphasic strategies in solo sailors.[1]

A 1992 study by Thomas Wehr found men kept in 14 hours of darkness daily settled into two sleep blocks with waking between.[1] A 1989 field study of 99 sailors concluded that polyphasic strategies improved sustained performance, though military and aviation reports note performance on ultrashort sleep stays below fully rested levels.[1] NASA-supported nap research by David Dinges found longer naps were generally better and nighttime naps could cause sleep inertia lasting up to an hour.[1] Sleep medicine bodies such as the Sleep Foundation say the schedules lack support for claimed productivity benefits and risk sleep deprivation, according to Grokipedia, which is AI-generated.[2] The NSF consensus panel report discusses adverse impacts.[3]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: On T Nation, members have asked whether polyphasic sleep could aid recovery or let them cope with long training and study days. One poster described getting by on five hours with two or three short naps and noting increased appetite; another started a thread on whether multiple naps could yield more REM sleep in less time.[5][6] Others in training threads have suggested that the body can adjust to as little as two hours of sleep, while replies elsewhere raise concerns about overtraining and recovery.[7][8]

Posters also discuss milder options such as coffee naps and a single daytime nap alongside a shorter night.[9] These variants sit closer to biphasic sleep, which the NSF panel's review excluded from its scope of nap and siesta schedules.[3]
Chronic sleep restriction, circadian misalignment and microsleeps during waking hours have been described.[1][2] Involuntary polyphasic sleep also occurs in irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder.[1]

A 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus panel screened more than 40,000 publications, retained 22 papers on polyphasic schedules, found no evidence supporting benefits, and associated such schedules with adverse health and performance outcomes.[3]

A 2024 study in Sleep restricted ten healthy young participants to one 20-minute nap opportunity every four hours with no core sleep window; the authors report that growth hormone release was abolished under sustained restriction.[4]
Earlier work includes Claudio Stampi's 1989 field study of sailors and a 1992 darkness study by Thomas Wehr, as summarised in encyclopedic sources.[1]

lore.intro: Polyphasic sleep appears in T Nation training and recovery threads and in productivity communities, where members compare schedules and ask about adapting to very little sleep.[5][6][8][10]

claims.claim: Short naps can replace most nighttime sleep and free up hours.
Pre-industrial humans naturally slept in segments, so polyphasic sleep is natural.
Polyphasic napping can support recovery for training in far less sleep time.
